description: A black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner. It is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.

hero.hook: Nothing gets out, not even light. And yet we ended up photographing its shadow.

blocks.text: A black hole is a region of **spacetime**, the fabric that ties space and time together, where gravity is so intense that the speed needed to escape is greater than the speed of light. Nothing leaves it: no matter, no light.

It is not a “hole” in the sense of a tunnel. It is an extreme concentration of matter that bends that fabric very hard. For a long time black holes were pure theory, a result of Einstein's equations. Today they are observed in several ways.

A stellar black hole is usually born from the death of a very massive star, at least **20 to 25 times** the mass of the Sun. While it lives, the star holds together through a balance: gravity pulls inward, and the pressure of **nuclear fusion** pushes outward. In the core of the star, hydrogen turns into helium.

blocks.caption: A black hole ringed by its glowing accretion disk

blocks.text: When the fuel runs out, the pressure collapses. The core of the star caves in. A **supernova** explosion can then light up the whole galaxy. If the leftover core is massive enough, nothing can stop the compression.

At the center, theory describes a [[gravitational singularity]]: a point where density and curvature become extreme, and where our current equations stop working properly. Around it lies the [[event horizon]]: an invisible boundary. Cross it and there is no way back to the rest of the universe.
If you fell toward a black hole, gravity would pull far harder on your feet than on your head. Physicists call that stretching “spaghettification.”

Despite the cliché, a black hole does not suck in everything that passes at a distance. Its gravity depends on its mass and on distance, just like any other object. If the Sun were swapped for a black hole of the same mass, the Earth would keep orbiting. Without light or heat, though, we would freeze.

There are also **supermassive black holes**, from millions to billions of solar masses, at the heart of almost every galaxy. In the Milky Way it is **Sagittarius A***, about **4 million** solar masses.

We often spot them thanks to the [[accretion disk]]: a ring of gas and dust whirling around them at huge speed. Friction heats that matter until it shines fiercely in X-rays or radio waves. The black hole then shows up as a shadow against that bright background.

In **April 2019**, the Event Horizon Telescope project released the first image of a black hole. By combining eight radio telescopes through [[interferometry]], the researchers built a virtual telescope the size of the Earth.

The target was **M87***, the supermassive black hole of the galaxy Messier 87, **55 million** light-years away. The image shows a bright ring around a dark zone: the silhouette of the event horizon. In **2022**, an image of our own neighbor Sagittarius A* followed.
Since **2015**, the LIGO and Virgo observatories have also been detecting **gravitational waves**: tiny vibrations of spacetime produced when two black holes merge.

In **1974**, the British physicist **Stephen Hawking** showed that a black hole would not be entirely black. Because of quantum effects near the horizon, it should give off a very faint glow: [[Hawking radiation]].

So a black hole left on its own would slowly lose mass and eventually evaporate. For a stellar black hole that would take spans of time fantastically longer than the current age of the universe. The idea also raises the information paradox: what becomes of the information about everything that fell in, if the black hole disappears?

Close to a black hole, time also runs more slowly as seen by a distant observer, a relativistic effect called **time dilation**. These objects remain among the best laboratories we have for testing the limits of physics.
A black hole often forms when a massive star collapses. Its edge is the event horizon, a boundary photographed for the first time in **2019** around M87*.
